title: Ibn Battuta leaves Tangier
hook: he leaves home alone for the Hajj, and the road keeps going (Rihla)
tomorrow: what did a traveler see on a Friday in Mali?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasan al-Basri's letter: the shepherd's care, measured by the flock. Today, a new part: travelers, and one who walked away from his own.

Travel videos open on a sunrise over a new city, never on the goodbye at the front door. Ibn Battuta's book does it backwards. Before a single wonder, he describes leaving Tangier: no companion to cheer him, no caravan to join, his parents still living, and a parting so hard that both they and he were stricken with grief. Why would a travel book begin in tears?
screen: `THE SUNRISE, NEVER THE GOODBYE.` → `NO COMPANION, NO CARAVAN.` → `WHY BEGIN IN TEARS?`

segments.voice: Because the reason was bigger than the grief, and he wants you to feel both. In his Rihla, his book of travels, he says he set out alone, moved by a strong pull inside him and a longing he had carried a long time: to visit the holy places, to make the Hajj. So he steeled himself, he says, to leave his dear ones, and he left home the way birds leave their nests. That picture solves the puzzle. A bird doesn't leave the nest because the nest is bad. It leaves because it has grown into something that has to fly. The goodbye is in the book because the love was real. The Qur'an speaks of the Hajj as a duty owed to God, in Pickthall's words, “for him who can find a way thither.” Ibn Battuta found a way, and paid for it in goodbyes. The Hajj was his destination, but the road kept going, years of it, through lands he couldn't have pictured from Tangier, and the book was later set down from his telling. It all begins with one man at the edge of his city, sad and sure at the same time. Alone, on the road.
screen: `A PULL STRONGER THAN THE GRIEF.` · `LIKE BIRDS LEAVING THEIR NESTS.` · `FOR WHOEVER CAN FIND A WAY.` · `SAD AND SURE AT ONCE.` · then, large: `ALONE, ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Stand up and take a few slow steps toward a door or a window, as if setting out on a long road. With each step, name one small thing that would move a goal of yours forward. Then come back, sit, and stay with the last one you named.
screen: `A FEW SLOW STEPS.` · `ONE SMALL THING PER STEP.`

segments.voice: Ibn Battuta leaves Tangier: the opening of his Rihla, a traveler setting out alone for the Hajj, grieving and certain.
What stays with you: alone, on the road, sad and sure at the same time. See you down the road.

howItsDone: Muslims setting out for Hajj often visit family to say goodbye and ask forgiveness before they leave; Ibn Battuta's Rihla is read as a classic of Muslim travel writing.

chat.says: booked the college visit up north. ALONE. first time flying solo. dad says he's fine. he's not. now what
options: Let it be sad and sure at once. Ibn Battuta grieved leaving and went; tell your dad both.
Act like it's no big deal. If you show it's hard, your dad will only worry more.
Maybe wait a year. If leaving hurts this much, it means you're not ready yet.
chat.meaning: Ibn Battuta's Rihla opens with grief at leaving his parents and a pull strong enough to go anyway; he tells both honestly.
